Question: What is the difference between O-levels/GCSEs and below O-levels/GCSEs? Which would I be if I was in year 10 and haven’t completed my GCSEs yet, but plan to?
Answer: The big difference is that O levels (which originated in the UK, in the late 1940s) haven't existed here since 1988, though they survive in some countries. If you are in the UK, Year 10 is normally your first year of GCSE work, and you take the exams in Year 11. Year 10 doesn't mean the same here as it does in countries such as India, so there's room for confusion. If your family plans to go back to India partway through your GCSE courses, it will be complicated, because GCSE syllabuses aren't even all the same in the UK between different exam boards, and definitely not the same between countries, and between GCSE and O level. The standards should be very similar, but the content won't be. Try to stay in one place while doing your GCSEs, and your A levels.

Question: Does lying require more effort?

As even Presidents and Princes have discovered, you can't fool all of the people all of the time. On balance, the truth, told at the right time rather than when it's dragged out of you, may be painful and embarrassing, but it's a whole lot easier, and in the long term, will involve much less pain and shame.

Question: If I want to get all grade 9s in my GCSEs, should I be revising in the summer after year 10?
Answer: Well, yes, some, but then, ideally you should have been doing a bit each week, ever since the start of Year 10. Likewise, a bit each week during Year 11 - and you can probably guess what I think you ought to do during Years 12 and 13. A bit each week, just looking back over the week's work, will help to fix it in your mind with no great effort. It also gives you the chance to go back and ask your teachers about anything you don't understand, missed or otherwise can't resolve. Then a half-term recap, and again at the end of each term, and the same at the end of the year. Second year, same as the first. But a little bit harder, and a little bit worse! Seriously, if you follow this kind of pattern, by the end of the course you will know all your work very well indeed. Now of course this is a counsel of perfection, a “don't do as I did, do as I say!” bit of advice. But maybe, if someone had said this to me 60 years ago, my exam results would have been quite consistently good, instead of being excellent in the things I loved, and a bit bleah in the things I didn't. I had the pleasure of a rare meeting with my cousin's son yesterday. He's American, 18, a really interesting person, and very definitely a smart kid. He accused himself of being lazy, and I said this was actually very normal for people like him; they're so used to everything being easy, that the hardest thing for them is learning how to work. I had the same problem, and perhaps you do too, OP. But if you follow the advice I've given you, then provided you can match work with ability, you should be on track for good grades all round. Success to you!

Question: If I want to enter the undergraduate program at Oxford, do I have to exceed the requirements of the university (for A level/IB)? Do universities treat those who meet the requirements equally?
Answer: Well, firstly, there's no such thing as “the undergraduate program” at Oxford, or indeed any UK university except possibly the Open University. You apply to study a particular subject, and the entry requirements will vary from subject to subject. If you are seriously interested in applying to Oxford, you really should have researched this already for yourself, rather than making vague assumptions and asking for the information; you couldn't possibly survive Oxford like this, and probably not even get in. Still, since you asked: you choose your degree subject, and go to either UCAS or Oxford’s website to find out their minimum, and typical, entry requirements. If you and your teachers think that you are likely to achieve those grades, then you go ahead and apply online, via UCAS (their website being Choose your future ), no later than the 15th October (the deadline is always the same), and ask your teachers to supply your Predicted Grades and a Reference. For some subjects, there are also assignments or tests set by Oxford as their own assessment of your eligibility. There is nothing automatic about your being accepted, even if your grades do look good enough; there's a fair way to go, yet. After that, you wait, and hope. If they think you look like a possible candidate, they will invite you for interview, usually around November, and this is the real test. You will have at least two very challenging interviews, for which all you can do by way of preparation is perhaps a practice interview or two, and get used to thinking for yourself. Because that is what will be needed in your interview; you will be faced with unexpected questions, and expected to think about them and respond intelligently. There's no question of learning things beforehand, so don't try. They're far more interested in your level of intelligent interest and ability to think on your feet, than in your subject knowledge. And then you go home and wait again. And some time around mid-January, you will find out whether or not you have been successful! I notice that someone else says that British students have a built-in advantage. Personally, I think they should have (it's a British university, after all), but in practice it seems that they don't; all the statistical evidence confirms this. So go for it. What is there to lose?

Question: How come in East Asian cultures dead bodies are more likely to be cremeated than put in graves to decay?
Answer: Sheer practicality, I think, as the initial motivation, but over a long period of time, practical considerations get coated with tradition too. And two major factors will be speed and space. Bodies start to decay quite quickly after death, and the warmer the climate, the faster decay sets in. Rotting flesh attracts flies, which lay eggs, which turn into maggots - it's not going to be pretty, and the smell is going to be awful, if you don't either refrigerate or otherwise dispose of the body, and fast. Refrigeration is pretty new. In the UK, along with other European countries, few people had an ordinary fridge in the kitchen before about 1960, just about 65 years ago, though they were fairly common in America earlier than that. And most countries in Africa and Asia still didn't have them for many years after Europe did, in fact many people in those countries still don't. What would be the point, anyway, if you don't have electricity to power such things? So refrigeration in morgues and undertakers’ premises were also not widespread. Arranging burials takes time, including finding somewhere suitable to bury the person who has died, and digging a hole deep enough and long enough. Cremation is fast, and the resulting ashes take up much less space than a coffin. A funerary urn of ashes can be buried, or the ashes scattered, but sometimes people just keep the ashes with them. Space is a major consideration, and in the UK at least, cremations are far more usual now than burials. I'm 71, and I can think of only 3 burials I've attended that were of bodies rather than ashes after cremations. As populations grow (and the world's population has quadrupled in my lifetime) available space shrinks, and full graveyards become a problem. So it's not just hot countries in Africa and Asia where cremations are usual - Catholic countries in Europe probably still prefer traditional burial, but in Protestant and secular countries (and the UK is both of these), even cooler ones, cremations make sense. Possibly America is the exception, rather than the norm? I'm just guessing, but if you are American, OP, and it's not the norm where you live, then remember that the rest of the world has reasons for doing things differently!

At this moment, there's no indication that you'd be likely to get grades like those - Bs and Cs are far more likely. But still, that's just statistical probability, not Predicted Grades. Also, get a voluntary part-time role in a local care home or hospital, or join the St John Ambulance Brigade, and stick at it; real commitment is what Admissions teams want to see, as well as the grades. If, in a year's time, you look like a good prospect for Medicine, then go for it. But if Medicine is slightly out of reach, there will be plenty of other things you could do instead, including things like Biomedical Science. So there's nothing to lose, and everything to gain. I hope it works out for you.

Question: Will the income from part-time jobs be sufficient for living and paying university fees in the UK?
Answer: Not a chance! Living and paying tuition fees in the UK will cost you around £30,000 per year, possibly much more. This means that you would need a pre-tax income of at least £40,000 per year, which is considerably more than most young university graduates earn, working full-time. There is no way you will be earning that sort of money in a part-time job delivering pizzas or working at the local supermarket (typical student jobs). In any case, you will be restricted to a maximum of 20 hours per week of working during term time. This is normal in most countries. Try to exceed that, and you're likely to get your visa revoked, and you will be deported. If you do try it, and start missing lectures or work deadlines as a result, your university has to report this, which makes it extremely likely that you will be caught. Besides, you have to pay your fees upfront, at the start of the year. And to get a visa at all, you'll need to demonstrate to the UKVI that you've got enough money in the bank to cover your whole expenses for the entire first year, and to assure them that you do not need to work in order to afford it. Once again, get caught lying to them and you can expect your visa to be revoked, and yourself deported. Coming to the UK to study is very expensive. Unless you really can afford it, I would strongly recommend that you stay at home!

Question: Why isn't English a Latin language?
Answer: Your grasp of the migratory history of Britain is a little tenuous. The Romans came. They stayed for a few hundred years (quite a lot of them weren’t actually Roman, but let it pass). They went away again (Well, most of them. Some had intermarried with local girls, and probably stayed, but most of them went). By about 407AD they had gone. Some of the Britons they left behind might have picked up a bit of Latin, but I doubt if they used it much once the Romans had gone and there was no-one to talk Latin to. Then the Saxons arrived, and the Angles, and the Friesians, and the Jutes, from Germany, Friesland, Jutland or assorted other places just across the North Sea. Being basically German, they spoke a form (well, several forms) of German. And having come, and finding no Romans to be difficult about it, they stayed. Their Germanic language drifted away from its roots a bit (rather like American English having drifted away from the English English of a few hundred years ago) and developed into what is now called Old English, but which people used to call Anglo-Saxon. And that stuck, pretty well, until about 1100, 1200 even. There had been Vikings along the way (they spoke what we now call Old Norse, but it was a sort of harsh cousin of Old English, so they could understand each other) and then in 1066 the Norman French arrived. They were basically of Viking stock too, but their ancestors had gone the long way round and settled in France, so they now spoke a form of French - which was descended from Latin, as you know. And as they won the Battle at Senlac (confusingly known as the Battle of Hastings) and were now in control, French became officially the language of government. But still, there were only a few thousand Normans at Senlac, and many times that number of Saxon descendants spread all over the country as a whole. So although Latin genes now crept into the language, it took a very long time for them to get well established. And there were always a lot more Saxon (and Viking, and Celtic) genes in the system than Norman French ones. It took several hundred years for the two languages to merge properly. It only starts to look a bit like a recognisable, blended language by about the time of Geoffrey Chaucer, in the late 1390s. So there you are. That’s why English isn’t a Latin language - because most of its ancestors weren’t Roman. Edit: I thought (hoped) I’d explained this clearly enough, but have just had someone saying (in effect), “But what’s the difference, it’s still just from Latin, isn’t it, like French?” So here, just to show it a different way, is the prettiest language family tree I have ever seen: English Language Family Tree You’ll notice that both the Romance branch (which includes all the Latin-based languages) and the Germanic branch start off from the European branch. You can get more detailed views of some of the main branches here: A language family tree - in pictures . So English is mainly descended from the same set of ancestors as German. But because it has spent time with, and has married into the same family as, French, it has picked up some French and Latin characteristics that show through, even though they’re not the main ancestral line. Does that help? I do hope so.
